stimulus.text: Historian David Potter describes the 1850s as the decade when 'the slavery question ceased to be a subject of debate and became a test of loyalty' — each section demanding the other prove its good faith.

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE issue that deepened sectional hostility between North and South in the period 1835–1860.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND such issue.
C. Briefly explain ONE effort to compromise between the sections in this period.
exemplar: Northern abolitionism — pamphlets, petitions, and orators like William Lloyd Garrison — convinced many Southerners that the North meant to destroy their way of life.
The fight over slavery in the territories acquired from Mexico, from the Wilmot Proviso through 'Bleeding Kansas,' turned westward expansion into a sectional battleground.
Leaders repeatedly tried compromise: the Missouri Compromise (1820) drew a line at 36°30′, and the Compromise of 1850 patched the Union together for another decade.

stimulus.text: "British cruisers have been in the continued practice of violating the American flag on the great highway of nations, and of seizing and carrying off persons sailing under it…" —James Madison, war message to Congress, June 1, 1812 (abridged)

parts: A. Briefly explain the grievance Madison describes in the passage.
B. Briefly explain ONE reason some Americans opposed declaring war in 1812.
C. Briefly explain ONE immediate consequence of the declaration of war.
exemplar: Madison describes impressment: the British navy stopping American ships and seizing sailors, a violation of American sovereignty and neutral rights.
New England Federalists opposed the war because their region depended on trade with Britain and feared economic ruin from a British blockade.
The United States immediately launched invasions of Canada, beginning with the failed 1812 campaign from Detroit.

stimulus.text: The diagram shows the triangular trade of the 1700s. One arrow runs from New England to West Africa labeled 'rum and manufactured goods.' A second arrow runs from West Africa to the West Indies labeled 'enslaved Africans (Middle Passage).' A third arrow runs from the West Indies back to New England labeled 'sugar and molasses.'

parts: A. Identify and briefly explain ONE pattern shown in the triangular trade diagram.
B. Briefly explain ONE way the British imperial system affected the colonies.
C. Briefly explain ONE way the colonies resisted greater British control.
exemplar: The diagram shows a three-legged circuit: New England ships carried rum to Africa, traded it for enslaved people, and returned with sugar and molasses from the West Indies. The pattern reveals how deeply the northern colonial economy depended on slavery even where plantations were rare.

One way the imperial system affected the colonies was through the Navigation Acts of 1660 and 1663, which forced colonists to ship tobacco, rice, and sugar to England and to route European goods through English ports, enriching English merchants at colonial expense.

Colonists resisted tighter control by smuggling and by defying royal authority — Massachusetts's defiance of the Navigation Acts helped provoke the Dominion of New England, and colonial assemblies used their 'power of the purse' to frustrate royal governors.
